clinicalPearls: Isopropanol causes central nervous system depression that is typically deeper and longer than an equivalent amount of ethanol
It produces ketosis without a significant metabolic acidosis, because it is metabolised to acetone rather than to an organic acid
There is a raised osmolar gap but characteristically a normal anion gap, distinguishing it from methanol and ethylene glycol
Acetone on the breath and ketonaemia with a near-normal glucose are useful clues
Gastritis with haematemesis and hypotension can occur after large ingestions
Management is largely supportive, with haemodialysis reserved for severe or refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Isopropanol is absorbed rapidly and metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone. Both the parent alcohol and acetone are central nervous system depressants, accounting for the prominent and prolonged sedation. Because acetone is a ketone rather than an organic acid, the result is ketosis with a raised osmolar gap but without the severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis seen with methanol and ethylene glycol. Direct mucosal irritation causes the associated haemorrhagic gastritis.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of coma with a raised osmolar gap
additionalInvestigations: Serum osmolality and calculation of the osmolar gap
Anion gap and blood gas (acidosis characteristically absent)
Serum and urine ketones and glucose
Isopropanol and acetone levels where available
Assessment for gastritis and haemodynamic compromise
redFlags: Hypotension or gastrointestinal bleeding after large ingestion
A significant metabolic acidosis, which should prompt reconsideration of methanol or ethylene glycol
reference.prognosis: With supportive care most patients recover fully; serious outcomes relate to profound central nervous system depression, aspiration, haemorrhagic gastritis or very large ingestions.
pitfalls: Assuming a high-anion-gap acidosis and misclassifying it as methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning
Overlooking the deep, prolonged sedation and airway risk
Failing to reconsider the diagnosis if acidosis develops
